tactics.title: Ad Hominem
tactics.definition: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself.
tactics.canonical_example: You can't trust his economic plan; he never finished college.

tactics.title: Strawman
tactics.definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack.
tactics.canonical_example: Person A: 'We should invest more in education.' Person B: 'Why do you want to leave our country defenseless by cutting military spending?'

tactics.title: False Dilemma
tactics.definition: Presenting only two options when many more exist; 'black-and-white' thinking.
tactics.canonical_example: Either you're with us, or you're with the terrorists.

tactics.title: Slippery Slope
tactics.definition: Claiming that a small first step will inevitably lead to a chain of related negative events.
tactics.canonical_example: If we allow students to redo one assignment, they'll soon expect to redo everything, and academic standards will vanish.

tactics.title: Hasty Generalization
tactics.definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from a small or unrepresentative sample size.
tactics.canonical_example: I met two people from that city and they were both rude, so everyone there must be rude.

tactics.title: Circular Reasoning
tactics.definition: The conclusion of the argument is already assumed in the premise.
tactics.canonical_example: The law is valid because it is the law.

tactics.title: Confirmation Bias
tactics.definition: The tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs.
tactics.canonical_example: A person who believes a certain health trend is effective only reads articles that praise it, ignoring scientific rebuttals.

tactics.title: Backfire Effect
tactics.definition: When presenting evidence that contradicts a person's belief actually strengthens that belief.
tactics.canonical_example: Correcting a political myth often causes the person to believe the myth even more strongly to protect their identity.
